name: Accessible Assessment and Adaptive Practice
title: Accessible Assessment and Adaptive Practice
answer: Accessible assessment means making tests measure what a student knows rather than their disability, with AI helping teachers create versions that use simpler language, larger print, audio, or different formats as allowed by a student's IEP. Adaptive practice can support IEP services, but it works as a tool within those services, not as a replacement, and progress must be checked outside the software. The teacher and team keep the decisions about whether an accessible version still measures the same skills and whether the tool is helping.

sections.body: This idea addresses two connected problems in special education: tests that measure a disability instead of knowledge, and practice tools that may be mistaken for a full service. AI can help teachers produce accessible versions of assessments, such as simpler language, larger print, audio, or different formats, when the IEP allows it. The teacher then checks that the accessible version still measures the same skills, because an accommodation that changes what is being measured is no longer an accommodation. Adaptive practice can be a valuable part of IEP services, giving students practice on goal skills. The lesson is to use it within services, not as a replacement for them.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, AI can help teachers create accessible assessment versions with simpler language, larger print, audio, or different formats, as allowed by a student's IEP. The teacher checks that the accessible version still measures the same skills. Adaptive practice can be a valuable part of IEP services. A special education teacher might use Zearn or Khan Academy for practice on a student's goal skills, while still providing direct instruction. Progress should be checked with measures outside the software, and the team decides whether the tool is helping.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports that a review of 29 studies found a medium sized effect for students with disabilities (Zhang, 2024). Some individual trials have reported very large effects, such as a randomized trial of 70 boys aged 9 to 12 with mild intellectual disability (Alsolami, 2024) and a study of 42 elementary students with math learning disabilities (Wang, 2025). Effects that large deserve caution, especially since a review of 11 studies of students with learning disabilities found that none had a low risk of bias (Paglialunga, 2025).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text: an accommodation that changes what is being measured is no longer an accommodation, so the teacher must check that an accessible version still measures the same skills. Adaptive practice should be used as a tool within IEP services, not as a replacement for them. Progress should be checked with measures outside the software. The team decides whether the tool is helping. The text also warns that very large effects deserve caution, especially because a review of 11 studies of students with learning disabilities found that none had a low risk of bias.
